entry.title: A Successfully Failed Instagram Social Experiment

link.title: A Successfully Failed Instagram Social Experiment

entry.content:
Introduction

I’m not going to present this in an academic way, because I want to share the idea more directly.

That was actually a thing happened about a month ago. My friend Astin posted this on Instagram:

Hi, my name is Astin. I believe a good amount of people know me, regardless of when or where our paths have crossed. Perhaps you should take part in this social experiment. The idea is to see who just skips through my stories and who pays attention. We are so focused on social media that we often forget the most important thing in life is relationships. If no one is reading this post, it will be a short experiment, but if you read this to the end, please send me a ‘hello’. I’ll then send this text to you with your name in it and have you publish it in your story. Don’t send me anything if you “don’t have time to post it.” It’ll ruin the purpose of this experiment. Let’s see who would be willing to expend their time to do it.

I found this immensely intriguing and immediately followed suit. While I was editing the copypasta, though, I noticed two issues.

  1. Noticeability. As this story spreads across different people’s accounts, it creates a recognizable pattern. If viewers see the same block of text repeatedly, they may learn the “correct response” and reply automatically without actually reading. That undermines the original aim, which is to check whether people stop and read the story.
  2. Forcibility. Once a viewer replies, they’re basically forced to participate. The line ‘Don’t send me anything if you don’t have time to post it’ works against the supposed goal. Someone might genuinely care but not want to repost (or just dislike chain posts), and this setup pushes them into an awkward choice: reply and feel obligated, or stay silent and look uncaring. Neither option helps the relationship.

Therefore, I made some modifications to the original copypasta and posted this to my story on 24 November 2025, 15:58:

Greetings, my name is Mason. I believe a good amount of people know me, regardless of when or where our paths have crossed. Perhaps you should take part in this social experiment. The idea is to see who just skips through my stories and who pays attention. We are so focused on social media that we often forget the most important thing in life is relationships. If no one is reading this post, it will be a short experiment, but if you read this to the end, please send me (1). I’ll then send this text to you with your name in it and have you publish it in your story. If you want to display that you care for me, but don’t have time to repost this or wish to opt out of the experiment, please reply me with (2). Let’s see who would be willing to expend their time to do it.

Here, (1) and (2) were placeholders of instructions, which were different per person. For example, the one set of (1) and (2) that I used in my story were:

(1): the result of one plus one in the written form

(2): the first word of the text

Below summarises the result.

Summary

The story ran for 24 hours.

# of viewers: I forgor

# of ‘two’s (including ‘unorthodox’ forms): 11+1

# of ‘Greetings’s (including ‘unorthodox’ and implied forms): 47+3

Responses that are unorthodox:

(Sending me a screenshot of him writing the Chinese character 二)

Grootings

not greetings

Sybau

(The N word)

PS I actually forgot a viewer’s name and inserted a pair of brackets (). I remembered her name the next day. Sorry!

Verdict

As implied from the title, this experiment comes out as a failure. The reason why I regard this as such is because it does not meet its aim, of which I will elaborate further below.

Reflection

Although improved, there are still some debatable points of this social experiment:

Homogeneity

The copypasta still follows the same structure: intro → instruction → more text → instruction. Aside from the placeholders, there isn’t much variation. When a viewer sees multiple stories of this kind, they will know what to respond before actually comprehend the full text as they can selectively read the instructions part.

One friend of mine, Enoch, actually mentioned this. He said that he had seen many stories of this kind prior to seeing mine. This actually means the stories are overly homogeneous, which creates a highly observable pattern.

Remember, the aim of this experiment is to test if viewers actually would bother to respond to stories to display genuine caring. However, if that care derives from merely reading a few words of a narrative without full understanding, that should not be caring, but rather robotic response.

Yet, what if the prompts for people to repost are customized for everyone? There might also be two problems. First, the running cost of the experiment will be too high (at least the time cost is), as one needs to vary the prompt for every single participant (ie those willing to repost the copypasta), or at least creates a number of variations that are noticeably distinct but still follow the aim.

This actually relates to the second problem. There will be deviations generated after multiple generations. As there is a possibility that people may overly change the prompts for the next generation, this amplifies the deviations from the original aim, which can give inaccurate results.

Validity

The original copypasta says:

The idea is to see who just skips through my stories and who pays attention. We are so focused on social media that we often forget the most important thing in life is relationships.

This assumes that people who don’t pay attention to stories are attached to social media and therefore neglect real relationships. However, there is no causation between attachment to social media and detachment from real-life relationships, albeit there can be correlation between so.

In fact, one can argue that people are fed up with social media, and choose to skim stories and posts. This situation actually means that there are potentially people who care for others and scroll away social media updates, which may lead to misjudgement on viewers’ actions.

Moreover, the following are also possible reasons that viewers do not respond to the story:

  • Busyness
  • Dislike of chained content
  • Missing of story by chance

It may be particularly perilous if the experiment conductors blindly determine that a particular person is not showing genuine care for them merely because of an inaction on social media.

On the other hand, does it mean someone who is active on social media and reads every single story also uses that much effort to listen to others? I doubt if that is the case.

Insecurity

By this, I don’t mean the data collection is insecure, but rather the mentality behind running the experiment.

When my friend Candies responded to me, they thought I was insecure. This is not the case for me, obviously, but can probably be the case for others if they are to conduct such an experiment.

Their doubt is sensible. Ordinary people do not post stories which are totally different from what they used to post, not to mention a social experiment to check if viewers actually respond to them. When someone conducts this experiment, this can make their followers think that the conductor is insecure about their relationships. This can hamper their relationships, as the linkage built upon trust and loyalty has been shaken.

Nontheless, this may be an economical way to check if friends are loyal and willing to show care. It usually takes a long period of time to determine if someone if loyal, and often one needs to have experienced different events to have known others’ personalities. This is reflected in a Chinese saying: 知人口面不知心 (‘you know people’s faces but not their minds’).

Yet, if it is cheap in time, it is to be expensive socially.

Conclusion

I am not really a big fan of social media, as I am too lazy to update. Yet, this social experiment on social media, although kind of failed, did provide new insights on the nature of social relationships.

Comment below to let me know your thoughts!

Perhaps i should sleep now bye

entry.title: Google Gemini updates: Flash 1.5, Gemma 2 and Project Astra

link.title: Google Gemini updates: Flash 1.5, Gemma 2 and Project Astra

entry.content:
Learn more:Learn more:Learn more:Learn more:Learn more:Learn more:May 14, 2024 We’re introducing a series of updates across the Gemini family of models, including the new 1.5 Flash, our lightweight model for speed and efficiency, and Project Astra, our vision for the future of AI assistants. In December, we launched our first natively multimodal model Gemini 1.0 in three sizes: Ultra, Pro and Nano. Just a few months later we released 1.5 Pro, with enhanced performance and a breakthrough long context window of 1 million tokens.Developers and enterprise customers have been putting 1.5 Pro to use in incredible ways and finding its long context window, multimodal reasoning capabilities and impressive overall performance incredibly useful.We know from user feedback that some applications need lower latency and a lower cost to serve. This inspired us to keep innovating, so today, we’re introducing Gemini 1.5 Flash: a model that’s lighter-weight than 1.5 Pro, and designed to be fast and efficient to serve at scale.Both 1.5 Pro and 1.5 Flash are available in public preview with a 1 million token context window in Google AI Studio and Vertex AI. And now, 1.5 Pro is also available with a 2 million token context window via waitlist to developers using the API and to Google Cloud customers.We’re also introducing updates across the Gemini family of models, announcing our next generation of open models, Gemma 2, and sharing progress on the future of AI assistants, with Project Astra.Context lengths of leading foundation models compared with Gemini 1.5’s 2 million token capability1.5 Flash is the newest addition to the Gemini model family and the fastest Gemini model served in the API. It’s optimized for high-volume, high-frequency tasks at scale, is more cost-efficient to serve and features our breakthrough long context window.While it’s a lighter weight model than 1.5 Pro, it’s highly capable of multimodal reasoning across vast amounts of information and delivers impressive quality for its size.The new Gemini 1.5 Flash model is optimized for speed and efficiency, is highly capable of multimodal reasoning and features our breakthrough long context window.1.5 Flash excels at summarization, chat applications, image and video captioning, data extraction from long documents and tables, and more. This is because it’s been trained by 1.5 Pro through a process called “distillation,” where the most essential knowledge and skills from a larger model are transferred to a smaller, more efficient model.Read more about 1.5 Flash in our updated Gemini 1.5 technical report, on the Gemini technology page, and learn about 1.5 Flash’s availability and pricing.Over the last few months, we’ve significantly improved 1.5 Pro, our best model for general performance across a wide range of tasks.Beyond extending its context window to 2 million tokens, we’ve enhanced its code generation, logical reasoning and planning, multi-turn conversation, and audio and image understanding through data and algorithmic advances. We see strong improvements on public and internal benchmarks for each of these tasks.1.5 Pro can now follow increasingly complex and nuanced instructions, including ones that specify product-level behavior involving role, format and style. We’ve improved control over the model’s responses for specific use cases, like crafting the persona and response style of a chat agent or automating workflows through multiple function calls. And we’ve enabled users to steer model behavior by setting system instructions.We added audio understanding in the Gemini API and Google AI Studio, so 1.5 Pro can now reason across image and audio for videos uploaded in Google AI Studio. And we’re now integrating 1.5 Pro into Google products, including Gemini Advanced and in Workspace apps.Read more about 1.5 Pro in our updated Gemini 1.5 technical report and on the Gemini technology page.Gemini Nano is expanding beyond text-only inputs to include images as well. Starting with Pixel, applications using Gemini Nano with Multimodality will be able to understand the world the way people do — not just through text, but also through sight, sound and spoken language.Read more about Gemini 1.0 Nano on Android.Today, we’re also sharing a series of updates to Gemma, our family of open models built from the same research and technology used to create the Gemini models.We’re announcing Gemma 2, our next generation of open models for responsible AI innovation. Gemma 2 has a new architecture designed for breakthrough performance and efficiency, and will be available in new sizes.The Gemma family is also expanding with PaliGemma, our first vision-language model inspired by PaLI-3. And we’ve upgraded our Responsible Generative AI Toolkit with LLM Comparator for evaluating the quality of model responses.Read more on the Developer blog.As part of Google DeepMind’s mission to build AI responsibly to benefit humanity, we’ve always wanted to develop universal AI agents that can be helpful in everyday life. That’s why today, we’re sharing our progress in building the future of AI assistants with Project Astra (advanced seeing and talking responsive agent).To be truly useful, an agent needs to understand and respond to the complex and dynamic world just like people do — and take in and remember what it sees and hears to understand context and take action. It also needs to be proactive, teachable and personal, so users can talk to it naturally and without lag or delay.While we’ve made incredible progress developing AI systems that can understand multimodal information, getting response time down to something conversational is a difficult engineering challenge. Over the past few years, we’ve been working to improve how our models perceive, reason and converse to make the pace and quality of interaction feel more natural.Building on Gemini, we’ve developed prototype agents that can process information faster by continuously encoding video frames, combining the video and speech input into a timeline of events, and caching this information for efficient recall.By leveraging our leading speech models, we also enhanced how they sound, giving the agents a wider range of intonations. These agents can better understand the context they’re being used in, and respond quickly, in conversation.With technology like this, it’s easy to envision a future where people could have an expert AI assistant by their side, through a phone or glasses. And some of these capabilities are coming to Google products, like the Gemini app and web experience, later this year.We’ve made incredible progress so far with our family of Gemini models, and we’re always striving to advance the state-of-the-art even further. By investing in a relentless production line of innovation, we’re able to explore new ideas at the frontier, while also unlocking the possibility of new and exciting Gemini use cases.Learn more about Gemini and its capabilities. entry.title: Displaying External Posts on Your al-folio Blog

link.title: Displaying External Posts on Your al-folio Blog

entry.content:
External Posts on Your al-folio Blog

If you prefer publishing blog posts on medium.com or other external sources, starting version v0.5.0, al-folio lets you to display your external posts in the blog feed of your website! 🎉🎉

Configuring external sources of super simple. After upgrading to v0.5.0, just add the following section to your _config.yml:

external_sources:
  - name: medium.com  # name of the source (arbitrary string)
    rss_url: https://medium.com/@<your-medium-username>/feed

The example above adds your medium.com blog post feed as an external source. But you can add arbitrary RSS feeds as sources.

Any questions or suggestions? 👉 Start a discussion on GitHub!
